entries.title: Egg
body: The book follows the egg from enclosed possibility to a world taking shape: cosmic eggs divide into earth and sky, while the shell shelters a life that cannot yet survive outside it. Incubation suggests a necessary interval of withdrawal before emergence.

Its alchemical reading places an almost invisible germ of renewal inside ordinary matter. Attention and warmth help latent life develop; the image joins containment with eventual release. This wider egg entry enriches the atlas’s more specific philosophical egg.

entries.title: Star
body: Stars give bearings to travelers and become images of small lights within psychic darkness. The polar star adds a different quality: an apparently still center around which a changing world turns.

The book contrasts guiding light with constraining fate. Astrological patterns may be imagined as compulsions, yet recognizing a pattern can also make a different response possible. Its alchemical stars suggest dispersed sparks gradually gathered into a more coherent center.

entries.title: Sun
body: Solar radiance carries vitality, creative power and conscious illumination. Crowns, halos and golden alchemical images borrow its authority, making the sun a figure for a center that sustains and orders life.

The same brightness can scorch or overexpose. The book uses myths of excessive solar aspiration to examine inflation, then turns to the aging alchemical sun: its renewal requires moisture, darkness and a lunar counterpart rather than endless intensification of light.

entries.title: Moon
body: Waxing, disappearance and return make the moon an image of change that includes loss. The book relates lunar rhythms to bodily moisture, fertility and decay, and to a form of knowing that measures phases rather than insisting on constant clarity.

The lunar vessel can carry the dead or hold a tranquil fullness. Its hidden aspect also draws the psyche beyond familiar awareness: that journey may deepen self-knowledge, or leave a person adrift in fascination. The moon therefore includes danger as well as nurture.

entries.title: Ocean / River
body: The ocean entry imagines a small conscious vessel surrounded by immense generative depths. Those waters sustain life, but their storms and engulfing force also evoke emotional conditions that exceed the vessel’s control.

The river gives water a direction and a channel. Its current becomes time, transition and a boundary to cross; sacred rivers can cleanse and revive, while the same flowing element can sweep a traveler away.

Read together, the entries distinguish immersion in an encompassing depth from movement toward another shore. Neither image is a simple promise of purification: passage requires a workable relation to a living, sometimes destructive medium.

entries.title: Wind
body: Invisible wind becomes perceptible through what it moves. The book follows its associations with breath, speech, spirit and inspiration, including the Navajo Windway and the feathered serpent’s union of aerial and earthly life.

Wind can enliven and connect, yet it arrives with its own direction and force. The sailor’s response offers a practical image of relationship: one adjusts to the current rather than assuming inspiration can be commanded.

entries.title: Fire · surviving continuation
body: The surviving continuation moves from Agni’s hearth warmth to fierce divine fire and the crafts of potter, smith and alchemist. Fire makes and destroys; its transformations cannot be reduced to either comfort or catastrophe.

Alchemy’s sulphurous fire becomes an image of affect and desire that can consume a person or bring hidden substance into a new form. Refinement requires a relation to that heat, including its power to melt, harden and clear away exhausted material.
This supplied PDF repeats printed pages 84–85 where 82–83 should appear. These notes use the surviving printed page 84 only; the missing opening of the Fire entry has not been reconstructed.

entries.title: Stone
body: A raised stone can mark a god, an ancestor or enduring remembrance. Its resistance to change supports images of permanence, while a stony heart or petrified body expresses an equally durable incapacity to respond.

The book turns from outer monument to an unknown interior. In alchemy, a commonplace, devalued stone may become the lapis: what appears inert contains a possibility that must be discovered through work on one’s own substance. Boundaries, union and embodied transformation meet in the stone.

entries.title: Mountain
body: The mountain offers height, distance and pilgrimage, but also a vast bodily mass whose streams nourish the surrounding world. The book brings its summit’s revelation into relation with its interior caverns, minerals and hidden gestation.

A mountain can join worlds as an axis or sacred meeting place; a volcano or underworld entrance gives the same form a threatening aspect. The entry keeps these culturally different readings in view rather than treating every ascent as a universal spiritual advance.

entries.title: Cave
body: The cave shelters early habitation and sacred images, opening a passage into the earth. The book brings womb and tomb together: descent may return a person to a source of life, initiate a transformation or lead into the realm of the dead.

Psychically, enclosure can allow incubation and retreat. It can also narrow the field of vision or become crushing confinement. Stories of Amaterasu, Plato’s prisoners and birth in a cave place the appearance of light against that dark interior, giving refuge and revelation different meanings.

entries.title: Salt
body: Salt’s capacity to dissolve, season and preserve makes it a meeting point of body and understanding. The book connects shared salt with hospitality and covenant, then traces how the savor of experience becomes an image of discrimination and wisdom.

Alchemical salt carries the bitterness of tears and disappointment as well as the possibility of cleansing. Its paradox is essential: what nourishes at one concentration can destroy at another. Transformation therefore involves proportion and assimilation, not simply removing everything bitter.

entries.title: Tree
body: Rooted in the earth and branching into the air, the tree gives growth a visible structure joining depth and height. Its seasonal losses and returns make renewal an ongoing rhythm rather than a single final attainment.

Yggdrasil’s roots, well, serpent and eagle connect memory, the dead and the gods, while creatures continue to damage and sustain the tree. The alchemical tree likewise holds illumination beside ordeal: hidden treasure at the roots and luminous fruit above belong to one difficult development.

The book stresses that inner growth has its own timing. A balanced crown may image the joining of opposites, but a living tree returns to drying, shedding and fresh growth; completion remains part of a cycle.

entries.title: Garden
body: The garden begins with tending: touching soil, making room, feeding and pruning. Its enclosure offers a protected space for contemplation, and a central fountain, tree or deity may organize that space as an image of potential wholeness.

An entrance to the secret garden is often difficult to find; a Japanese garden may disclose itself gradually along a path. The book treats discovery as a relation that unfolds over time, not an interior already visible in a single glance.

Cultivation does not abolish autonomy. Growth surprises the gardener, and an untended enclosure returns to wilderness. The garden’s symbolic life depends on this negotiation between deliberate care and forces that exceed domestication.

entries.title: Lotus
body: The lotus rises from muddy water into an open flower. The book reads this as continuity between dense, changing conditions and luminous awareness: emergence does not require denying the medium that nourished it.

Egyptian imagery reveals a solar child from a primordial lotus, while Indian and Tibetan images place deities, meditative centers and chakras in lotus forms. In the Buddhist example, the awakened figure is undisturbed by the changing world without being separate from it.

entries.title: Rose
body: The rose gathers earthly affection, sacred devotion, remembered loss and desire for something elusive. Its fragrance and layered petals allow the book to move between lovers, goddesses, the Virgin and alchemical images without assigning the flower one fixed meaning.

Red and white roses can join contrary natures, while the privacy of alchemical work resembles a life developing within closed petals. Thorns complicate the sweetness: they may protect what is vulnerable, or become a defensive barrier that prevents intimacy and growth.

entries.title: Snake
body: The snake evokes a life that moves close to the earth yet appears unexpectedly from hidden places. Its watchful eye and renewed skin support images of perception and transformation; its danger keeps those possibilities from becoming merely reassuring.

The book follows distinct serpent traditions, including kundalini and the sanctuary of Asclepius. Coiled power, dream incubation and the healing snake place renewal near death’s territory. Venom and cure belong to the same ambiguous creature, so guidance requires respect for its force.

entries.title: Fish
body: Paul Klee’s goldfish introduces a living image emerging from an unseen watery world. Rather than treating the unconscious as empty depth, the book considers its inhabitants: something with its own form can be encountered patiently and brought into awareness.

Christian fish and baptismal waters suggest restored participation, while the two Pisces fish carry a split between spiritual aspiration and material life. Alchemical fish eyes add small, persistent lights within matter, imagining a possibility of perception that can include both sides of that division.

entries.title: Bird
body: Birds travel between ground, water and air, making flight an image of communication between different realms. The book associates this movement with soul, inspiration and the creative passage from a perceived world to an inner image.

Flight is balanced by nesting, brooding, seasonal return and bodily song. Inspiration therefore includes listening to instinct and coming home, not only escaping weight. The entry places a soul’s guidance in the alternating movements of ascent, descent, reception and expression.

entries.title: Dove
body: The dove’s pairing, shared nest and gentle presence join love with fertile devotion. The book follows its appearances with love goddesses, the returning bird after the flood, and the Christian Holy Spirit as different forms of relationship and renewing arrival.

Alchemy’s dove moves both upward from dark waters and downward to meet them, mediating between aspiration and affect. Its apparent purity need not mean separation from ordinary life: the source also recalls the vulnerable, sometimes despised city pigeon beneath the exalted image.

entries.title: Crow / Raven
body: The book’s crows and ravens disturb convenient divisions between helpful and destructive. In Northwest Pacific Coast stories, Raven may bring light and useful knowledge through trickery while remaining capable of confusion and harm; Odin’s ravens probe the worlds as thought and memory.

The alchemical raven belongs to the dark phase in which flattering accounts of oneself are stripped away. Its scavenging image can feel humiliating, yet the birds’ ingenuity and play also disclose another kind of consciousness: perceptive, irreverent and hard to domesticate.

entries.title: Eagle
body: The eagle’s height and searching gaze attract images of sovereignty, solar power and far-seeing spirit. Its predatory force prevents grandeur from becoming an innocent ideal; the book keeps imperial violence and nurturing care within the same bird.

Alchemy gives ascent an answering descent. An insight that leaves the emotional ground behind can disappear into abstraction; the sea eagle’s plunge and return instead image illumination brought into embodied life. The eagle and serpent may oppose each other, but sky and earth also exchange nourishing waters.

entries.title: Peacock
body: The peacock’s radiant display evokes the sun, renewal and an apparently incorruptible life, while its burdened gait and harsh cry complicate the splendid surface. The book reads pride and vulnerability alongside the promise of resurrection.

Its many eyes and changing colors become images of enlarged vision and synthesis. Legends of turning a snake’s venom into luminous plumage suggest a symbolic transformation of poison into insight; the alchemical tail announces a new configuration of what was formerly divided.

entries.title: King / Queen
body: Royal figures embody the principles that govern a person or a community, carrying conscious authority together with powers that consciousness does not control. Sun and moon, gold and silver, throne and crown give that sovereignty a symbolic setting.

A wounded or aging ruler reveals an order that no longer nourishes its land. The book reads alchemical King Sol and Queen Luna as a union that changes both partners and ends the former arrangement; renewal may also arrive through a humble helper close to instinct.

entries.title: Crown
body: A crown concentrates radiance at the head, linking earthly authority to solar vitality. Its many gems can image diverse qualities brought into relation, and the crowning of a lowly figure can recognize a worth larger than familiar ego status.

The book also follows the crown’s weight: responsibility, anxiety, destiny and the piercing crown of thorns. To be crowned can therefore expose a person to a demanding office or suffering as well as confer splendor.

entries.title: Dragon
body: The dragon combines aerial and earthly powers that ordinary animals keep apart. Chinese cloud-and-water dragons give this composite a nourishing, seasonal life, while dragon-slayers confront an engulfing force. These traditions make its meaning depend on the encounter.

Alchemy’s winged and wingless dragons stage conflicts between volatile vision and embodied substance. Their poison can become medicine through the work; the treasure-bearing dragon also images a hidden process capable of initiating renewal before the conscious personality understands it.

entries.title: Mandala / Labyrinth
body: The mandala entry centers on Tantric Buddhist practice. A palace, its directions and its deities connect world and practitioner; guided visualization and initiation work through that ordered space toward transformation of body, speech and mind. The geometry belongs to a living ritual context.

The neighboring labyrinth entry offers a different experience of center: from above the path has order, while from inside it confuses and doubles back. In the Chartres example, circle, cross and central flower join a Christian journey of transformation.
This is an editorial comparison of two named book entries. A center can orient a person without making the route direct; the book’s labyrinth asks how confusion can gradually enlarge perspective.

entries.title: Crucifixion
body: This entry concerns the crucifixion image, especially its Christian setting, rather than every cultural form of the cross. The suspended body intensifies isolation, suffering and the tension of opposed demands that cannot be resolved by an easy choice.

The book connects alchemical crucifixion with surrender of an exhausted form of consciousness, but refuses to guarantee redemption. Some suffering becomes meaningful; some remains destructive. The image marks a radical alteration whose consequences cannot be assumed in advance.

entries.title: Pearl
body: A luminous treasure hidden in an ordinary shell becomes an image of something precious within embodied life. The book follows the pearl through Persian soul imagery, the Gnostic return to self-knowledge and Chinese dragons retrieving wisdom from mist.

Its symbolic attraction also rests on a persistent irritant gradually clothed in new substance. The entry uses that growth to imagine suffering taking on meaning over time; it is a possibility of transformation, not a claim that every wound automatically produces a treasure.

entries.title: Grail
body: The Grail can appear as vessel, abundant nourishment and the elusive goal of a quest. The book moves between a cauldron of plenty, Christian communion and medieval romance, allowing the sought object to take different forms rather than restricting it to one cup.

The quest involves detours, dangerous crossings and help beyond personal mastery. The wounded Fisher King makes the goal relational: healing restores the life of a realm. An enclosed garden and a rose flowering from the vessel join source, center and the gradual growth of an inner life.

entries.title: Butterfly / Moth
body: The butterfly is the book’s image of the soul renewed out of confinement: the chrysalis is both vessel and thing transformed, showing nothing outside while the old form dissolves. Settings stay apart: Australian Aboriginal returning souls as caterpillars, Aztec heroic dead, and an Eastern pupa that models serene growth.

Its fluttering casts a shadow of anxiety, inconstant desire and compulsive devouring. Yet brief lives and the moth’s self-consuming pull toward light make both insects images of ardent longing, which the book sets beside Eros and Psyche, where desire is self-destructive as well as promising.

entries.title: Frogs
body: Water, womb and fertility are the frog’s field. The book ties it to Heqet, the Egyptian midwife goddess of embryonic waters, and to a very old frog goddess; frogs appearing from Nile silt are read as unformed matter and the passage from dying to being born again.

Settings divide: early Christian lamps proclaim resurrection, while later Christians heard an unclean, witch-linked spirit. In dreams and fairy tales the frog surfaces suddenly and must be accepted as a frog before it becomes prince or princess. The book closes on frogs as early signals of an environment out of balance.

entries.title: Necklace
body: In myth the necklace is the goddess’s attribute: her beauty, attraction and fecundity, its circle the unity of her world and its many beads the multiplicity of life. The book reads Freyja’s Brisingamen and the smith Hephaistus marrying Aphrodite as the source-goddess meeting the craftsman who gives her earthly form.

Settings differ. Hathor is present in her menat; skull and snake necklaces mark the destructive side of Shiva and Kali; shamans take a totem animal’s power by wearing its teeth, while a collar means subjugation. The necklace also guards throat and heart, and in dreams a breaking or theft asks what bond it carried.

entries.title: Scorpion
body: The scorpion stands where fluid depth meets firm ground, an old image of passage. The book offers the Egyptian goddess Selket, a scorpion mother who carries her young and guards the dead, as a threshold figure holding both the sting of death and its antidote.

The same creature carries dread: a fiery tail marks the Maya war god and the Christian devil. Even so, sting and renewal belong together, since the book sets the scorpion among the oldest emblems of the Great Mother, venom and remedy at once, with mating where fruitfulness stands beside annihilation.

entries.title: Weaving / Spinning
body: Weaving is making from one’s own substance, and it begins in the divine world, so a small flaw is worked in as a reminder of imperfection. The book follows the loom as an image of existence, crossing time and space and the visible and invisible, and finds cloth kin to speech in Dogon myth and Homer’s weaving women.

Spinning carries destiny: the Norns beneath the world tree, and the Greek spinners who spin, measure and cut life’s thread. Thread stretches like time, and the moon measures time and fate in her phases. Captions add a Christian Virgin with spindle and a Greek ivory spinner as separate settings. The link to the spindle family is an editorial comparison: the book’s entry is its essay on weaving and spinning.

entries.title: Crab
body: The essay starts from an Armenian image of a crab holding the full moon: admiring a mirror, or about to devour it and begin its waning. Crab and moon are counterparts, rising, advancing and retreating together and linked with mother, night, water, feeling and the inconstant.

Regression is not only negative: the moon’s dark brings renewal, and the unconscious’s dark can carry rebirth in the sea-mother’s womb. The shell is double, defence over insecurity or a firm boundary around what is vulnerable. As Cancer, the crab marks midsummer’s turn and the home instinct for refuge.

entries.title: Bull
body: The essay starts from a tiny Indus seal in which a zebu’s eyes and horns face the viewer, force rather than anatomy. The book ties the bull to civilization’s beginnings, with cattle feeding communities and drawing the plow, nature’s power harnessed yet never under human control.

Its range touches all four elements and above all water, in Shiva’s horns and the Nile flood. Nandi holds the god’s destructive and generative sides together, and Dionysus, torn apart as Zagreus and reborn, is read as sheer life force. Psychologically the bull is instinct met as other, and Taurus a practice of tending it.

entries.title: Goat
body: The goat is the cunning, independent animal the cooperative sheep is not, hard to contain and unsettling to look at. Its leaping, otherworldly look ties it to darkness and untamed passion, yet domesticated it nurtures: Amalthea suckles Zeus, and the goat is a sign of fertility and virility.

The book follows its darker projections: the devil as a goat-man, and the scapegoat loaded with sin and driven out, which the essay answers with conscious acknowledgment of one’s own shadow. Pan renews passion when reflected on and compels when not; too much order leaves us open to him.

entries.title: Scale
body: The essay opens on a final judgment in which Michael and the devil contend for souls, weighed in a pan while a demon tugs the balance. The book reads soul-weighing across traditions as the idea that attitudes and principles have real substance; Egyptian images set the heart against Maat’s feather, Ammit waiting below.

Other settings gather: the Kabbalah’s Ancient of Days holding the scale from which duality came, blindfolded Justice, and Libra at the equinox. Symbolically the scale is poise among psychic opposites, though a level balance is not always possible; psyche answers one-sidedness by tipping into the opposite.

entries.title: Great Cats
body: The lion, tiger, leopard and jaguar form one company of great cats, whose prestige rests on strength, grace and sumptuous presence, with an ambivalence mirrored in their coats. The lion is solar, golden and sovereign, an Egyptian horizon sentry and Sekhmet, the sun’s watchful or raging eye, while alchemy’s Green Lion devours the sun and draws the mind downward.

Each cat takes its own place: the tiger’s warrior spring, the leopard of shamans’ treetop journeys, the jaguar of eclipse and the underworld. They are wild and can devour. A great cat prowling the home in a dream warns of identification with raw energy, and caging it is repression; the essay looks for balance and boundaries. The link to the Lion family is an editorial comparison with the book’s wider Great Cats entry.

entries.title: Air
body: The essay opens with an Egyptian headrest on which the air god Shu lifts the king’s head between lions. As the book reads it, air is what lies between earth and heaven and holds them apart, yet it also acts as go-between, bearing prayers upward and light and divine commands down.

Air is breath and atmosphere, a medium of spirit and soul that is double: it carries sound and disease, feeds fire and flame, brings rain and hurricane. Symbolically airiness is quickness of mind or lack of ground, sublimation in alchemy, and room for relating instead of identifying, a way to catch one’s breath.

entries.title: Tower
body: The essay begins with de Chirico’s entranceless tower which has no door and no horizon and still shows something built that reaches skyward. Ziggurats, pyramids and stupas are towers modelled on the cosmic mountain at the world’s centre, a longing to return to heaven, as the Luba myth has it; towers also became the means by which a society keeps chaos at bay.

The ascent is double: the book finds Babel’s warning of hubris echoed in the Twin Towers and financial collapses, while the shattered tarot tower’s falling sparks suggest new creative life. The interior can imprison yet allow reflection; the ivory tower means isolation, while far sight and solitary endurance serve Psyche and the fairy-tale heroine.

entries.title: Wheel
body: The essay starts from the sun wheel as a form of the circle of totality, its hub an ambivalent center and its spokes measures of time and space. Tibetan Buddhism’s Wheel of Life shows rebirth in the grip of impermanence, and the alchemical opus circles through ascent and descent toward a hidden center.

Brought down to earth, the wheel stands between concrete and imaginal, and its images are double: potter’s wheel and millstone, the spinning wheel of fate, the torture wheel of agonizing compulsion and the rut. The Plains medicine wheels keep a meaning the essay says is unknown, perhaps sun ceremony or healing. The link to this card is an editorial comparison: the book’s entry is its essay on the wheel.

entries.title: Hanging
body: The essay opens with the Norse poem of Odin hanging nine nights on the world tree, offering himself to himself, and with a custom of hanging men and animals as offerings to him. Other hangings stand beside it: a figure inverted by one foot, read as initiatory surrender; Judas hanged in self-loathing, with demons waiting below; Peter asking to hang head-down.

The essay also turns to hanging as legal punishment, still lawful in some American states, and as communal violence in lynching. These are set beside the sacred hangings without being reconciled into a single meaning. The link to this card is an editorial comparison: the book’s entry is its essay on hanging.
